alt: The toolkit of 3.1 the sociological approach and 3.2 structures, processes and issues feeds into the two topics, 3.3 Families and 3.4 Education. Research methods, 3.7, runs underneath both and is examined across both papers.
caption: Learn the toolkit once, then apply it to families, education and methods.

alt: Three cards. Functionalists Murdock and Parsons list primary socialisation, stabilisation of adult personalities, reproduction and economic support. Marxists say the family reproduces labour power, passes on property and is a unit of consumption. Feminists focus on patriarchy, split into liberal, radical and Marxist feminist views.
caption: Set the perspectives against each other: they disagree about whom the family serves.

alt: Two panels. Zaretsky, a Marxist, says the family benefits capitalism: the idea of a separate private life is an illusion and unpaid domestic labour props the system up. Delphy and Leonard, feminists, say the family benefits men, who exploit women’s work, so it maintains patriarchy.
caption: Zaretsky blames capitalism; Delphy and Leonard blame patriarchy.

alt: Four reasons, changes in the law, changes in social attitudes and values, secularisation and the changing status of women, feed into the rise in divorce since 1945. The Divorce Reform Act 1969, in force from 1971, allowed divorce for irretrievable breakdown and was followed by a sharp rise. Consequences fall on husbands and wives, children and the extended family, including more lone-parent families.
caption: Four reasons explain the rise in divorce; its effects reach the whole family.

alt: Three stacked class layers with an arrow pointing down: stratified diffusion means changes spread from higher to lower classes. Below, family roles move from segregated, clearly divided roles to joint roles in a symmetrical, home-centred family. A note adds Oakley’s dual burden and Duncombe and Marsden’s triple shift.
caption: Young and Willmott saw symmetry spreading down the classes; Oakley disagreed.

alt: Three stacked columns showing a woman’s load. Young and Willmott’s symmetrical family: paid work and shared housework. Oakley’s dual burden: paid work plus most of the housework. Duncombe and Marsden’s triple shift: paid work, housework and emotional work.
caption: Each study adds a layer: from shared roles to the dual burden to the triple shift.

alt: A school building holds internal factors: labelling, streaming, subcultures, an ethnocentric curriculum and teacher expectations. Outside it are external factors: material deprivation, cultural capital, parental attitudes and language codes. Ball sits across the wall, with work on both sides. Below, achievement by class, gender and ethnicity.
caption: Sort every explanation: inside the school gates, or outside them?
